utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There was -- there are two preliminaries. Mr. Lukic, I understand that you would like to spend 50 minutes on Mr. Kecmanovic. That request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President, and good morning. Your Honours, for the second time this week we received an updated exhibit list for a witness the morning he was scheduled to testify. Yesterday morning now. In this case, the additional document that was added is 62 pages long in the B/C/S, 77 in the English, and it appears the final page in the B/C/S may be missing from the English. And I would just ask, as I did on Monday, for an explanation why we received such late notice that the document would be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us the additional document, what is it approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the Islamic Declaration and the 65 ter is 1D00172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any explanation, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic, not now, not during the rest of the day. Never. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is uploaded into the system as 1D172. I think it's been there for a long time. And only actually in the preparation with this witness I realised that I should speak about this document with the witness, since he was present in Sarajevo with Alija Izetbegovic for a long time and I think that he can give us an insight. And if the Prosecution needs more time we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you need it, but could have been foreseen. Mr. Traldi, the document may not be entirely new to the Prosecution. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right. It's not entirely new to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll proceed and allow Mr. Lukic to refer to the document, but it's clearly put on the record now that you object against this late -- not late disclosure but at least late notice of this document to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, and to the pattern of it that may be developing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may just to add one thing. We had numerous times that the Prosecution changed their list a day before the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's the reason why we are so relatively relaxed about it, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- also knowing that it is not something that was totally unknown to the Prosecution. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time to put the following on the record. Pursuant to the Prosecution's responses to the Defence Rule 92 ter motions for Milutin Vukicic dated the 1st of July and Milan Pejic dated the 10th of June, 2014, the Prosecution has requested that portions of the witness statements for Witness Vukicic and Witness Pejic be excluded on the basis that they contain tu quoque evidence. The Chamber would now like to invite the Defence to respond, either orally or in written form, to the Prosecution's objections as set out in the aforementioned responses no later than Wednesday, the 16th of July. I continue. On the 15th of May, the Defence filed a motion pursuant to Rule 92 ter seeking the admission of a statement of Witness Milorad Sehovac and a number of associated exhibits. On the 29th of May, the Prosecution filed its response, not objecting to the Rule 92 ter motion but opposing the admission of certain associated exhibits. On the 4th of June, the Defence filed a request for leave to reply with its reply attached as an annex. The Chamber hereby grants leave to reply. Next, in its response on the 29th of May of this year, the Prosecution opposed the admission of the associated exhibits listed as Rule 65 ter numbers 1D02057 and 1D02058, requesting the Defence to correctly identify and upload the documents in e-court. In its reply, the Defence stated that the correct 65 ter numbers of the documents referred to in paragraphs 52 and 53 of the statements are 1D02527 and 1D2528. The Chamber would like to know whether the Prosecution objects to the admission of the correctly identified documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kecmanovic. Before you give evidence the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Kecmanovic. Mr. Kecmanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, I take it that you'll finish during this first session, if there are not too many interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Me too, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just ask the usher to help us. I want to hand the statement to Professor Kecmanovic. And we can have on our screens 1D1633. That's the statement Professor Kecmanovic has in front of him in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps start with asking the witness for stating his name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you heard it. I forgot to ask you to state your first and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see before you on the screen and in hard copy the first page of your statement. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the last page as well. We see on the screen the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You provided this statement to the Defence of President Karadzic and of General Mladic as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that we agreed to remove paragraph 54 of the Karadzic statement because you are to testify as fact witness concerning the municipality of Prijedor, that was the case in the Karadzic proceedings, but you have no personal knowledge of the events there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask the same questions of you today that you addressed in your statement, would you basically provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one correction that was made in the Karadzic case that I don't think has been here. In paragraph 8, there is a reference to the witness -- what I believe to be the witness's party and it's translated as Serbian Radical Party, SRS, rather than SRSJ, and I wonder if it could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you remember that you were asked about it in the previous proceedings. There was some confusion with the abbreviations; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was stated that it was the Serb Radical Party, but what was the real name of your party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation was the same, SRS, but it was the Alliance of Reform Forces, and thus -- and there was confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1633 receives number D556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I took it that by making that one observation that there was no objection, therefore D556 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you to my learned friend for raising this and giving us the opportunity to correct this. Thank you, Your Honours. Now I would like to read short summary from Professor Kecmanovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: May Mr. Lukic read slowly as the booths have not been given a copy of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to speak slowly since the booths have not received a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. It's a short one so I think I won't create big trouble for the booths. Nenad Kecmanovic was a member of the B and H Presidency from April 1992, when the Serb politicians left that body, until July 1992. Nenad Kecmanovic will testify about the political crisis in B and H that led to the war. He will testify about the division of political power in B and H after the first multi-party elections. Furthermore, he will testify about the relationship between the SDS, SDA, and HDZ, as well as about the arming of Muslims and Croats before the outbreak of the war. Nenad Kecmanovic will testify about the functioning of the B and H Presidency after the beginning of the conflict and about the peace plans. And Professor Kecmanovic will testify about the situation and events in Sarajevo before and after the outbreak of the war. And that was the short summary. I have some questions for Professor Kecmanovic, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we won't be long, but we need to go through some of the issues. Please tell us briefly what was the sequence in which the ethnic parties were founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first party to be formed was the Party of Democratic Action, next it was the Croatian Democratic Union, and last the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to see 1D172 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we are going to see the Islamic Declaration on our screens shortly. Are you familiar with this paper?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who authored it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was this pamphlet received by the non-Islamic peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was much concern due to a number of theses stated in the paper. For example, there is reference made to the impossibility of joining Islam with non-Islamic institutions, and also that the Muslims, for as long as they are a minority in a state, need to adjust themselves to the constitution and the laws, and at the point in time when they -- their numerical strength is sufficient to make them a majority, at that point they are to impose a Muslim order or Muslim theocracy of sorts, in which minority peoples would enjoy limited rights. Some compared it to the situation of the Ottoman empire rule in Bosnia when the non-Muslim peoples enjoyed lesser rights than the members of Islamic -- the Islamic community. The second edition of the declaration appeared in 1990. That is an important fact. The first edition was published 20 years before. When the first edition came out, Izetbegovic was an unknown, a clerk in a construction company with a legal background. He worked on administrative tasks. But at the moment of the second edition's publication, Izetbegovic was already the leader of the most numerous ethnic group in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in relative terms, plus the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, as now, had the largest birth rate, and the numerical ratio between the three groups kept changing in favour of the Muslim community. And as the leader of the most expansive group, he published this declaration -- republished this declaration proposing that the Muslim population impose an Islamic theocracy, which was rather terrifying for a relatively minority -- or minor group as the Serb one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how did Alija Izetbegovic see Serbs in a future Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did he see them? Without expanding it much further but I could already see it at the time when I was a member of the BH Presidency. I worked on a platform, a programme document, which I initiated which was supposed to elaborate the goals of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That document, which I initiated while working alongside a group of colleagues in the Presidency, delineates or, rather, focuses on the establishment of a House of Peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina and one of the theses was that there should be parity in the Presidency of BH, including all three peoples with each having the right of veto. In the parliament it would be done through the House of Peoples and in the Presidency by quality representation and the right to veto. The first comments about the draft of the platform, when distributed to the other members of the Presidency, and when there was discussion, Izetbegovic put his main objection as saying that we can see from the text that the Muslims were in the majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I responded by saying that it was the only way for Bosnia-Herzegovina to function, that all three constituent peoples needed to be on an equal footing. Otherwise, the state would not be acceptable for the other two peoples without that precondition. Despite that explanation, he still objected, and we added that it was the tradition which existed at the time where such mechanisms may not have been institutionally drafted but were nevertheless put into practice. There was always consideration for the ethnic key, even in institutions which were not directly related to politics. For example, the school of political science where I worked, the dean was always chosen on the ethnic key principle. In other words, all three ethnicities had their representatives rotating at the helm of the school and the same applied to Sarajevo university and other universities in the country, although there were fewer back then. However, the principle was the same. The same was in place for the president of the arts and sciences academy and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please put focused questions to the witness because part of what he says is already in his statement and we don't need to hear it twice. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, please tell us what is Uma?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Uma is also something Izetbegovic mentions in the Islamic Declaration. At some point he says that small- and medium-sized ethnic states are not strong enough to be political players, but that it is faith that unites the Muslim people. He discusses Uma, which is a sort of Muslim or Islamic community which would be above any of the states as an umbrella organisation which would encompass Muslims from Morocco to Indonesia. It was supposed to be a cultural and political alliance of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the status of Serbs in Croatia in the fall of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly put, the Serbs were deleted from the constitution. Until then they had been a constituent people in the Republic of Croatia, following which they were excluded from the constitution. They were demoted from a constituent people to the status of an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did that influence the reasoning and activities of Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was still a single country, despite it being already in the process of deep disintegration. In that situation, the Serbs in Bosnia also felt concern, fear that something of the sort could take place in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, given the fact that there too they were in a relative minority. It was only natural to expect that it would stir the thinking, the consciousness of the people, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few words on the internal borders in Yugoslavia. What was the nature of internal borders, in terms of the republics?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the period between the wars, we called administrative or internal borders. They did not have state character. They were based on convention and treated as such until the 1960s. At the time when the borders were created at the end of World War II, when peace was reintroduced following 1945, there were several options tabled that were later dropped. For example, Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, in one variant, was to be seen as a third autonomous province within Serbia, and a part of the Communist leadership, including Mosa Pijade, I believe, who represented that variant, was outvoted as compared to the other members of the leadership. And one of the opposing group leaders was Djilas. They were rather in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina being a separate republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For those who don't know that, what was the ethnic background of Mosa Pijade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rankovic, you mentioned in line 10 of page 12?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian. If you allow me, let me add, it is a well-known fact how those internal boundaries or borders were treated. For instance, a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first variant which was adopted officially, part of Montenegro, Herceg Novi, the town which is a coastal littoral town in Montenegro, was seen as part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After it was adopted, a year later, the leader of Montenegro, Blazo Jovanovic asked Djuro Pucar, who was the Communist leader of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he asked him, given that Montenegro was small in territorial terms, to give them Herceg Novi town and surrounds, and Djuro Pucar granted him his wish. And that correction was subsequently introduced and then it was legalised, and it was considered legal and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Alija Izetbegovic think that war was more -- that peace was more important or separation of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you hint at his much-quoted statement before the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was quoted as saying he would favour sovereignty even if it meant war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about visits by Alija Izetbegovic to other countries in 1991? Do you remember his first visit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His first visit to Ankara -- was to Ankara, he went to Turkey first. And what was memorable about that visit, which caused an incident, is that while there, he applied on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina for introduction or joining the Conference of Islamic Organisation or the International Islamic Organisation although he had not been given a consent from the other two sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It even led to an incident of sorts because Nikola Koljevic, who -- when it came to internal division of labour and remit within the Presidency, who was in charge of foreign relations, but he had not been informed about this, neither was the Presidency, but Alija Izetbegovic, when hearing objections about that, he explained it in this very naive way: Well, I understood the Division of labour was that the Muslims would lead the Presidency, the Serbs the Assembly, and the Croats the government, which was a very naive explanation for such a move on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a brief question about this. Do you know Mr. Zulfikar Pasic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him personally as well as Mr. Izetbegovic and other prominent protagonists of these developments. As far as Adil Zulfikarpasic is concerned, at the very beginning, he was involved in establishing the SDA, the Muslim political party. He was among the leaders. He was one of the two vice-presidents. His importance lay in the fact that during the communist regime, he helped Muslim dissidents. He funded the legal fees and defence of Alija Izetbegovic before court. He established an Islamic institute in Zurich which was a refuge for Muslim dissidents. He appeared in Sarajevo on the eve of -- of the reconstruction or revival of multi-party system. He approached me with an idea of establishing a multi-ethnic political party. He would lead it. I was offered a place for vice-president on behalf of the Serbs. I don't know who he planned for the Croat side. Although he had created many favours for Alija Izetbegovic, he split from Alija Izetbegovic very soon, citing religious conservatism and fanaticism within the SDA. He explained it in that way. After that he established his own political party, which bore no Islamic or Muslim characteristics. The name was Bosniak -- Muslim Bosniak party. It was a lay party. However, it wasn't very successful at the ballot box. Some parts of the Muslim elite joined it, but it wasn't very appealing to the voter. At the same time, he was one of the Muslim leaders who showed to be most in favour of a peaceful solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, for a peaceful settlement. He was part of an unfortunately unsuccessful arrangement with the Serbs in Bosnia, with Slobodan Milosevic. That agreement shows -- has two titles. First is the historic agreement and the other title is the Belgrade initiative. It was a project whereby Bosnia-Herzegovina would be -- remain part of a truncated Yugoslavia and would be on equal footing with Serbia and Montenegro, who had opted to stay within Yugoslavia. One of the solutions was to make Alija Izetbegovic the first president of such a truncated Yugoslavia. Alija Izetbegovic supported that initiative, but on the eve of its publication, a conference, televised conference, was convened. I was there as a representative of the opposition parties, and Izetbegovic was supposed to come back from a trip. He showed up, and he said, live on TV, that the SDA would withdraw -- would like withdraw from that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. We will have to speed things up to shorten your answers. We know that professors are even more talkative than lawyers. Could you please briefly tell us what happened in October 1991 in the political life of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is arguably one of the turning points. I presume by this you mean the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence. Well, this is an introduction to a -- a prelude to events which would break up Bosnia-Herzegovina and lead to war. Bosnia-Herzegovinians' independence was proclaimed despite the opposition of Serbian deputies in the Assembly. For the first time, a mechanism of the workings of Bosnia-Herzegovinian parliament was broken and that mechanism was council for a national equality. It was a substitute to the House of Peoples which worked at the -- following the following principle: If one delegation would oppose a move -- motion, then that motion would be deleted from the standing orders. For the first time, SDA and HDZ ignored Serbs' demands to strike it off the standing orders. They even ignored the fact that Serbian deputies walked out and that decision on BH independence was adopted. It wasn't just about that event but the importance was that ethnic equality was violated. The principle was violated, and the Bosnian Serb people and the deputies saw that as a change in behaviour in political life, and that it was an introduction of a different climate where one of the three constituent nations would be made less equal or that those mechanisms for equality would be systematically violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the majority during the voting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it a two-thirds majority?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Neither was it achieved in all the subsequent votes, which is requisite for such decisions which is also applicable to the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know specifically that the outcome was 64 per cent in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina's secession. Of course, you needed 66 per cent for that to be a two-thirds majority. So it's simply incredible how you could violate and ignore such a violation, which is apparent in mathematical terms and how the international community also ignored that fact, including the Badinter commission and other European institutions who chose to ignore that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, immediately after that, what was the reaction of the HDZ, after, in October 1991, together with the SDA, when they voted for BiH independence?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking - and I could illustrate this through many examples but I'm trying to be brief - it was a tactical move of the HDZ, as I see it, and they used that tactic later on. On the one hand, they would show solidarity with the SDA, but at the same time they made moves which were symmetrical to Serb moves. Then a couple of weeks ago, they started creating Croatian autonomous districts such as Serbian autonomous districts. For instance, there was the Herceg-Bosnia autonomous district and then there was another one, HAO, of central Bosnia, where there were large concentrations of Croats among the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained how the right to veto was commonplace in political life of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When Koljevic and Plavsic left the Presidency, you were co-opted into the Presidency. Did you seek that the rule of consensus and the right to veto be introduced?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the precondition for my joining the Presidency because it had been demonstrated earlier that there was constant outvoting. For that reason, Serbian representatives left the Presidency. This was the reason. I demanded that we have consensual decision-making, which implied the right to veto of course. Another condition I put, not the only one, that all members of the Presidency freeze their party political functions, and the third demand was that the government be changed, which was incompetent. But my first and primary condition was to introduce right of veto and consensual decision-making. Then Izetbegovic had two weeks to mull it over and then he accepted those conditions, but later on he systematically violated those demands. If you like me, I can illustrate this through a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this principle apply in the political life of Bosnia-Herzegovina still?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As I initially said, I introduced that principle into the political platform that we were engaged in drafting before these events, because this was -- in June 1992 was accepted by the whole Presidency. And even today, this document is being mentioned as a document, as a platform that could have stopped or prevented the war. In the Dayton documents, this principle which is contained in the principle on which I insisted as a condition for my joining the Presidency, this is still valid, the three-strong Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina needs to be unanimous or there is a veto, so if there is no unanimity, there is no decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the term of office of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic limited or unlimited?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, first of all, did not become a president of the Presidency regularly. Fikret Abdic should have been that by law because he received the largest number of votes, but the circumstances dictated that president -- Alija Izetbegovic become president and I can explain those circumstances. His term of office was one year. He was a chairman of a collegiate body. He was a primus inter pares. He had a one-year term of office with the possibility of extending that term for another year, but as you know, Izetbegovic continued to -- in this post, contrary to the constitution, throughout the war and even in the post-war years. Constitution dictated that in 1992, or towards the end of 1992, he should have been replaced by a representative of the Croatian people. That was the system, the ethnic key.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's discuss recognition of the republics. When was the Badinter commission supposed to reach their decision on the recognition of Slovenia and Croatia, and the conditions for recognition of a republic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards that decision, which was supposed to have been made by the Badinter commission, when did Germany recognise Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It took place in Maastricht at a European-level meeting. According to the contemporaneous information and the documents I read subsequently, it was a sort of blackmail, a forced decision, opposed by the Americans, but that was the meeting when decisions were made on the common currency, and Germany preconditioned that condition by recognising the two republics first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina which took place on the 29th of February and 1 March 1992, save for the percentages you mentioned, saying that there was no two-third majority, was the voting itself legitimate without the participation of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it was illegitimate. In a way, the Serb Democratic Party - actually by that time we could already refer to it as the Serbian National Movement - in a certain way expressed its own political will about the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They had organised a plebiscite before the referendum but the mechanism was the same. Thereupon, the Serbs and possibly individual representatives of the other two peoples voted in very high percentages, over 90 per cent, in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia. Simply put, the Serbs boycotted the referendum. They did not vote except in individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Badinter commission proposed certain conditions for the holding of the referendum. Were the conditions met? And if not, what was not met, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Badinter solution, it was envisaged that a majority of all three peoples would have to be in favour of that decision but that was not honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The government which declared independence on 3 March 1992, did it include representatives of all three peoples?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The BH government? Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serb representatives vote in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Briefly, on the Cutileiro Plan, did it envisage a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all other peace plans for Bosnia-Herzegovina envisage a division in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is interesting to look at it from this point of view, when considering political developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, that division was made more dramatic. It was always discussed in the context of something that would destroy Bosnia-Herzegovina from the inside, and I was following it, that is why I can testify to it and I was also a direct participant through the political bodies. Starting with the Cutileiro Plan, which included the opposition parties as well, and there was always this reference made to this -- the separation. There was a map expert always close on hand to Cutileiro, a British person, whose last name I can't recall, but I think he died in the meantime. All subsequent plans, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Contact Group, and finally the Dayton Accords all make internal division operative, as if there was no alternative. No one then discussed the notion of unified Bosnia. Even the representatives of the Muslim people discussed it as a fully legitimate proposal and preliminary -- made preliminary agreements to a possible arrangement. For example, Izetbegovic initialled the Lisbon agreement which included it. And then all of a sudden, it became an anathema, something that ran completely contrary to the interests of the Muslim people, simply putting forward the proposal that no such Bosnia would be possible. Some of those agreements even referred to a particular solution which would be to the extent that Republika Srpska would be allowed to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina after a few years, much as confederation was discussed as a topic between the Muslim and Croatian community in order for the Croats to join Croatia as a confederate state. So there were two different solutions placed on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Bosnian pre-war calendar, what took place on 9 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the 6th of April? I don't understand. It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic at some point issue a general mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it on the 4th or the 6th, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any contacts between Izetbegovic and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serb representatives asked that the decision be withdrawn. It practically meant introducing war into Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that President Karadzic and the most senior leaders of Republika Srpska insisted on not taking that road. It was the first step to introducing a state of war and beginning a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, from that time, who was against demilitarising Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, the most radical person in that regard was Ejup Ganic, who is otherwise a curious figure on the Bosnian scene in the ranks of the Muslim community. He ran for president and was actually elected as a Yugoslav representative, supranational one, but he turned out to be one of the most radical SDA members, and he even enjoyed the status of Izetbegovic's deputy although not formally. He also objected to the Ohrid Agreement reached between the top echelons of JNA and leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was supposed to introduce an interim period within which for the first five years the JNA was to stay in BH territory but placing itself under the authority of the new leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then after the interim period, during which it would be in charge of keeping order, it would be disbanded, and the personnel was to freely choose where to go following that. I myself worked on that agreement, and travelled to Belgrade to discuss it. When it was all finally defined at Ohrid, and Blagoje Adzic was present at the meeting as the chief of General Staff and by that time defence minister, and there was also Alija Izetbegovic, Branko Kostic, as the president of Yugoslavia, and the host, Kiro Gligorov. When Izetbegovic brought the agreement to Sarajevo it was rejected, although he too took part in preparing it, on Ejup Ganic's insistence. He was against pacifying the situation in Sarajevo. His position was that it ran contrary to the objectives of the Muslim community, and that the Muslim community needed Sarajevo to be besieged because it was the spotlight of world media, and that they had to make sure to picture Sarajevo as a victim before the eyes of the world, the victim of Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think it was all we had for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just tender 1D172 to be MFI'd since I just learned that there is something missing, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's what appears to me from a quick look. I don't have any objection to it being MFI'd, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we have looked at the cover page and the photograph. That's the only thing we have seen from it. The witness told us what he considered to be relevant or at least -- therefore I wonder whether we need to learn by heart 77 pages, where the witness spent a couple of minutes on the matter. Of course, that's part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, he did discuss parts although I didn't open the specific pages but he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- comment on -- we can take out those pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you make an excerpt of the relevant portions which -- because otherwise we have to read all 77 pages, most of the pages, at least, I'm afraid, without any context for us. And there may be not that much disagreement about the existence of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't disagree about the existence of the document, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the content of it neither, that it is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We agree it is what it is, of course, and we are happy to talk to the Defence about which portions should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties -- if you could make a selection, Mr. Lukic, so that we find those portions where the witness referred to, and then if you would come to an agreement with the Prosecution about what we should read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the document for the time being will be MFI'd, awaiting both -- well, I do not know whether there is any need to complete the last page if the last page is not part of the excerpt, but at least waiting for further agreement of the parties of what is covered by the evidence of this witness and therefore to be read by the Judges. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D172 receives number P -- D557, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D557 is marked for identification. Mr. Kecmanovic, we take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break I would like to very briefly address one matter; that is, associated exhibits in relation to the Rule 92 ter motion of -- concerning Witness Milorad Sehovac. The Defence has tendered 21 associated exhibits for Witness Milorad Sehovac. The Chamber reminds the parties that it will not accept to be flooded with associated exhibits. This includes the length as well as the number of the tendered exhibits. The Chamber recalls that it prefers that documents are tendered during the witness's examination in court, which allows the witness to explain and comment on them. That's what I would like to put on the record. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier this morning the Trial Chamber inquired as to whether we had an objection to the correctly identified documents associated with Milorad Sehovac. We do not since -- now that they are correctly identified. That would be 1D02527, 1D02528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's on the record. Mr. Lukic, my observations in relation to the number of associated exhibits with Mr. Sehovac, of course, is also an invitation to reduce the number of associated exhibits and to deal with them -- with any exhibit with the witness himself and -- similarly as we did with the Prosecution, because you make a reference now and then to what we did in the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I don't remember that that proceeding was implied during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was several times --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Repeatedly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I remember a witness with 60 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that on good cause shown that no exceptions can be made, but the bottom line was a limited number of five was -- of course, we now and then allowed a bit more, sometimes considerably more, but we often also insisted very much on the reduction of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Traldi, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you've provided expert reports in two cases before this Tribunal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Kvocka case and the Simic case; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also appeared and testified as an expert in the Simic case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the reports you drafted, the information you provided was accurate and truthful to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In certain cases, which I pointed out, it happened, for example, when some locations are mentioned, that I received such information from others. It was second-hand information. Practically during the entire period before the war and the first few months of the war, I was in Sarajevo, so I have no knowledge applicable to any areas outside Sarajevo. Based on direct experience, that is. I generally assessed the situation within the political context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand that you're attempting to distinguish how you acquired different types of information. My question was simply: The information you provided in those reports, was it accurate and truthful to the best of your knowledge and your ability to ensure that it was accurate and truthful? Whatever source you acquired the information from.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you also gave a statement to the Karadzic Defence team; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like to look now at the one paragraph of your statement for the Karadzic case which is not included in your statement for this case. In paragraph 54 of that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 30943. It's page 28 in the English, and the bottom of page 20 in the B/C/S. This will be Mr. Kecmanovic's statement to the Karadzic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly zoom in on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page on the left-hand side, under the word "Prijedor." This paragraph reads: "As for the expert report for Prijedor, which I wrote for another case" - I think we will have to turn very soon to the next page in the B/C/S, at the top - "and in which I mentioned an incident in which two Serbian policemen were killed, I stand by what is written in my report. It says that the killing caused terrible repression by the Serbian army and police which ended with the expulsion of the Muslim population not only from that village but the neighbouring ones as well and with the torching of Muslim houses. In my report, I also described what happened in Omarska and Keraterm, saying they were place was highly inhumane conditions. I also stated that war crimes had been committed against individuals and groups of prisoners there. I would like to add that I gained my knowledge about these events during work tasks carried out with other experts who were better informed about what was going on locally. I have no direct knowledge of these events nor did I participate in them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement today, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I drew my conclusions based on the way I explained therein, saying that I had no personal knowledge but that it was second-hand information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what the statement actually says, Witness. So therefore, the question was whether you stand by this, of course, including those lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just for clarity of the record I think it's important to have an answer to the initial question. Do you stand by the paragraph that I just read from your Karadzic statement today? In its entirety.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in its entirety. Only the concluding part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you do not stand by the expert report you drafted for your earlier trial? For the Kvocka trial?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because in the meantime, I heard other information, since I spent quite a lot of time in the territory of Republika Srpska. People from the field pointed out to me that it wasn't quite as it was stated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That must have happened, then, since you gave your statement in the Karadzic case. Because in 2012, you did stand behind that report.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So let's just go through. Is it no longer your position that there was terrible repression by the Serbian army and police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that it is unavoidable in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you contest that there were inhumane conditions in Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, in prisoner camps, as far as I know, one doesn't encounter much humane principle applied because the institution per definition is not a very humane one and also as per definition conditions reflect that. I say so based on my presumption because I never spent any time in such camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you've also testified under oath that you admitted atrocities had occurred at those camps, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I spoke under oath, but the thing is much time has passed in between and in the meantime I acquired new information, new knowledge, which can relativise or rebut the information that I had received previously, because these are all second-hand information. What I testified about as being my personal knowledge, this I cannot change. But about those testimonies that are based on second-hand information, these can be changed by intervening second-hand information that I received in the meantime, and this may prompt me to change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's go through the sources of information you had had by the time you testified in the Karadzic case. You'd received reports while you were a member of the BiH Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I cannot take into account as relevant information that I received as member of the Presidency because those information were sort of wartime propaganda. If you give me time, I could explain how the Presidency really functioned, not nominally but really. The information that you insist on, I received later on in Belgrade via a person who resided in Belgrade at the time - I could tell you his name, unfortunately he's no longer alive - who hails that from that territory, who went -- used to go there and go back to Belgrade, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, again, you didn't directly answer the question I asked, but I take it from your answer that it's right that you did receive reports while you were a member of the BiH Presidency, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received the information that we absolutely could not rely upon. I even stated something to that effect in my statement. The information that we received came from mainly Sefer Halilovic, who, at the time, was Chief of the General Staff of the ABiH, and who was even a member of the War Presidency. And he would supply us with information to the effect that the Serb army was committing terrible atrocities, the Muslim civilians suffered great casualties, and as far as the military part of the report is concerned, he would keep reporting about huge successes on the part of ABiH. It was such implausible that -- so implausible that even Alija Izetbegovic asked him to present more realistic reports. So we kept hearing about terrible atrocities on the -- carried out by the Serbian army against Muslim civilians and successes -- a continuous stream of successes of the ABiH against the aggressor. Of course, this could not correspond to the truth, but the consequence of that was that none of us could really rely upon what we kept hearing from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I think the simple answer to the question was: Yes, you received reports. You chose not -- you choose today not rely upon them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. I think the witness said at that time he didn't have any trust in those information, not that he choose today not to trust them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the witness said that he received the reports. I think that part of your summary is right. And the witness said that for his report, he couldn't rely on it. I think he -- let me just take it -- take you back to -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may help, page 31, line 9, it starts, the answer: "We received the information that we absolutely could not rely upon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you did not rely upon it in your 2012 report, Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi. So the -- and you still do not rely upon it? That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to look, then, at some excerpts from the sessions of the Bosnian Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30954? This is an excerpt from the 133rd session on 30 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could I perhaps ask one additional question in relation to what the witness earlier said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you had -- you got information from a person who had -- in Belgrade, a person who had died. Could you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosko Baskot was his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think last year. He was very old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any way the parties could perhaps verify when this person died? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We will look into it, Mr. President. Could we have page 7 in the English and page 14 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. He was a communist official who had played an important role up to the half-point line in the -- in a period between the two wars and up to an extent until the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I only asked you when he died. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at the top of the page, we see the end of a comment of yours, the top of the page in the English. I believe it's toward the bottom in the B/C/S. And you've been talking about some Serbs who were detained in Sarajevo. You say: "To be frank, the more cases like this we have, the more we would indirectly tolerate this. Signing up to the anarchy that is happening on the other side, where the crimes are of course incomparably worse, genocide, et cetera" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's at the top, right above the word "Izetbegovic" in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "However, this does not excuse us anything in establishing the rule of law in the areas we control." Now, the other side would have been the Serb side at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this concerns also the Serbian and the Croatian side because at that time, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So it concerns both the Serbian and the Croatian side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. So it appears that at that time, you are discussing crimes, including genocide, being committed by the Serb and, as you say, Croat sides. So my question is: Were you relying on the reports you received as a member of the BiH Presidency or had you also acquired that information from other sources?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had opportunity to hear in the media, on the radio, for instance, foreign radio stations, who at the time, if I remember correctly, spoke about 300.000, as early as the first few months of the war, 300.000 Muslim casualties, because those reports coming from international media sounded much more plausible, more authoritative. When you are in such a position, you are impressed with such information. Of course you cannot verify them. And as you know, later on, even Muslim institutions and international institutions reduced that number from 300.000, not just Muslims, but to 100.000 of all Serbs, Croats and Muslims. And of course, at the time you had to select between what you believe and what you do not believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My question was simply: Were you relying on the reports you received as a member of the Presidency or also from other sources? And I understand you received reports as a member of the Presidency and also from other sources about the crimes being committed against Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: When such information were corresponding to one another, then I would show more confidence in them, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And one of the ways that the information corresponded is both of them reported massive atrocities against the Muslim population in various areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After I left Sarajevo, I received more credible information, and this is why I cited this example about the total number of casualties. Later on, subsequently, they were shown to be untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But for 20 years, from the time you left the Presidency till the time you gave your Karadzic statement, that continuing credible information did not change your view that inhumane acts, crimes, had been committed at camps including Keraterm and Omarska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I already discussed this, that I subsequently received information that these claims were overblown, and this is why I express now that I have a different attitude towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, when I asked you about the paragraph in your Karadzic statement, I didn't ask you about specific numbers of victims at either camp. What I asked you was whether you stood by your conclusion that you by then had expressed on multiple occasions, that crimes had been committed in Prijedor municipality, including those camps. So is your position that certain things you heard were overblown or that no crimes were committed there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That they were overblown, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so you continue to agree that crimes were committed in both of those institutions and in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the Presidency, the people discussing crimes against non-Serb civilians including those held in camps weren't just you and General Halilovic, they also included the Serb representative, the other Serb representative, Mr. Mirko Pejanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 10 in the English and 17 in the B/C/S, and it's towards the top of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic says in pertinent part: "I think we are reacting inadequately to this spreading and increase in the number of camps for Muslims in the republic. We are not doing enough to animate the public either in Bosnia or internationally." So Mr. Pejanovic again is informing the Presidency and discussing in the Presidency the increase and spread in camps for Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30954 receives number P6657, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, what's the size of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I admit, Your Honour, I don't recall off the top of my head but we are checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a lengthy document, that, of course, is the gist of my question, and do we need all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's an excerpt from the transcript. The B/C/S is 20 pages and the English somewhat less, 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12 pages, and it mainly deals -- the excerpt is focused on the questions you've put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've inquired about the parts I'm most interested in, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be? Oh, we already received the number, yes. Yes, we received the number. Then P6657 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the 30th of June isn't the first time that someone other than you or other than Mr. Halilovic, General Halilovic, discussed camps for non-Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Presidency, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 30th of June of which year, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 1992, Judge Moloto, as in the excerpt from the transcript we just looked at. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll ask my question again in case that would be useful. The 30th of June 1992, in the previous excerpt we looked at, that's not the first time that someone other than you, someone other than General Halilovic, discussed camps for non-Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Presidency, is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably no. Well, I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 30945. These are the minutes of the 117th session of the BiH Presidency on the 12th of June, 1992. And if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see a list of attendees and under members of the Presidency, we see your name; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Under items, or "taska," 1 and 2, I'm going to direct your attention to Dr. Musir Brkic's comments. And it says he: "... Explained the difference between immediate threat of war which is now in the BiH in force and proclamation of the state of war, and then" - and this will be the part that I'm asking you about - "pointed to the great problem regarding the arrested civilians who are being taken to Pale and other camps." Now, at this time Pale was in Serb territory; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was discussing camps run by Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And discussing the arrested non-Serb civilians who were being held there? Right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document, 65 ter 30945.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would then object since it's probably lengthy as well. So only the excerpt should be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know yet. I would have asked, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In this case, it's the minutes. It's four pages in B/C/S and five in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have the documents yet for the cross with me so I also don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may revisit the issue of the length if further studying the document would lead you to do so. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30945 receives number P6658, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you've suggested that these allegations were propaganda; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, you insisted on something what Musir Brkic stated, but you see, you have to take into account the following thing. When it comes to Mirko Pejanovic, he stayed in the Presidency all the way because he -- among other things, he thought about these things differently from me. And I left the Presidency, Pejanovic stayed there and lives there. You will notice that I insisted and discussed mistreatment of Serbs in Sarajevo because I immediately witnessed those things. What happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the issue. The issue is that you earlier said that these reports were propaganda, not how you responded to that propaganda, not what others thought, and that is what Mr. Traldi is now asking you, whether these allegations are propaganda or not, because you named them as such before. Irrespective of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, the question was how much confidence I had in what was provided as information. Everything was second hand because I wasn't in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you want to make your own statement apparently. I'll read the question to you: "Sir, you've suggested that these allegations were propaganda; right?" That was the question. Nothing else. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer, Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have confidence in those information. I saw them as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer, therefore, is yes. Whether you had confidence in them was not the question. The question was whether it was propaganda. You say: "I saw them as propaganda." That's the answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 09723? Now, this is an analysis of functioning of the RS MUP so far and the outlines of its furthers activities dated 11 July 1992. Could we turn to page 2 in both languages, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, at the beginning, we read: "The meeting was attended by the following people ..." We see Mico Stanisic's name and then a number of others. Those are all officials in the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those names there, those are all officials in the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior; right? Mico Stanisic, Cedo Kljajic, Slobodan Skipina, and a number of others?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the names do ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, you're familiar with Mr. Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was the minister of internal affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In a certain period of time, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That period of time included the 11th of July, when this meeting was held; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 8 in the English and I believe it's 9 in the B/C/S. It will be the top of 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Here we see part of Mr. Zupljanin's remarks, which began a few pages earlier. At the top of the page in the English we read: "The army and Crisis Staffs wartime Presidencies demand gathering as many Muslims as possible and leave such non-defined camps to the internal affairs. The conditions in these camps are poor. There is no food. Some individuals do not comply with the international standards because, among other things, the concentration centres are not appropriate or for other reasons." Now, I'd put to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should, for the benefit of the witness, also indicate where this is to be found on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My Cyrillic is a little bit imperfect, Your Honour, so it may take me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, did you find the portion Mr. Traldi read to you? Did you find the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my screen, it says: Several thousand court proceedings have not been completed, the courts are not operational, et cetera. In keeping with the regulation on subject matter jurisdiction of the courts, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It seems we may have the wrong page in the B/C/S. And I apologise for that, Your Honours. Could we perhaps go back to page 8? Here I think it may be the second bullet essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Does that correspond to the English I read you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now when I have the translation, actually, the original in B/C/S, I would object to the translation. It says "concentration centres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second, Mr. Lukic. If you want to discuss the content and the accuracy of the translation, I'd rather do that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or the witness can just read what is written so it should be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you know that usually verification of translation is not done by reading and then receiving interpretation. So, Mr. Traldi, is there any way that you could proceed and that we could discuss this later, that is, somewhere eight minutes from now, in the absence of the witness? If not, then we will just ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd guess --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing, I don't have this document on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have it on the bottom of page 2, and when I say "I have it," I mean of course that Ms. Stewart has it at the bottom of page 2 of our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I stand corrected. I'm semi-blind. I couldn't find it swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd suggest, since the words Mr. Lukic mentioned are not essential to my question, that perhaps we have CLSS check it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask the witness to read in his language and then ask whatever questions you'd like to put to him, and then later we can deal with the accuracy of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So could you read that second paragraph starting at: "The army and Crisis Staff," sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could you read aloud beginning at the word -- I think it's "Vojska"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, whenever the witness reads anything which is of concern to you, then please indicate so, Mr. Traldi, because there is a standard procedure, translations are not to be corrected by reading and then translating. Now, I do not know what -- where Mr. Lukic's problem is. I do not know what you want to draw our attention to, so not knowing the two, you can ask the witness to read aloud -- to read or perhaps you indicate already what you want him to read, and then Mr. Lukic will tell us whether he has any concerns with those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To start, sir, could you read the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that I saw the problem in the second-last row in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then the witness can read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The army and Crisis Staffs, wartime Presidency, demand gathering as many Muslims as possible and leave such non-defined camps to the internal affairs. The conditions in these camps are poor. There is no food. Some individuals do not comply with the international standards because, among other things, such collection centres are not appropriate or for other reasons." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, you've, I think in your enthusiasm, have read two sentences rather than one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Collection centres or concentration centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd suggest we have CLSS check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That seems to be the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it talks about centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of centres we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would suggest that this translation was a proper one, not the written one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that will be verified and we can proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, I wanted to direct your attention to a different part. This reports that the army and the Crisis Staffs, the political authorities, had demanded gathering as many Muslims as possible in camps with poor conditions, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This report comes from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As I noted, these are part of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin's remarks.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then it is probably authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please -- apparently you have a different agenda on your mind as just answering the questions. The question was the following: Mr. Traldi wanted to direct your attention to this report and this report says that the army and the Crisis Staffs, the political authorities, had demanded gathering as many Muslims as possible in camps with poor conditions. Mr. Traldi asked you whether that is what this paragraph at least in this portion says. Does it or does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it reads. I just read it out, out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it reads, that's what it says. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is around the same time you were receiving such reports as a member of the BiH Presidency, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I asked about, sir, is: Was this around the time that you were receiving such reports? We saw those in June, and this is in the first half of July; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
