utterances.text: There was a difference. In the reports we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not invited to compare the reports, whether they were different or the same, but whether such reports -- Mr. Traldi, perhaps you could clarify, you mean by "such reports," reports about detention situations of non-Serbs? Whether it was at the same time that you received reports, perhaps different, that wasn't the question, about detention of non-Serbs in camps or centres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me try and make it very simple. This is dated July 11th; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it reports the detention of large numbers of Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we've just seen that on June 12th and June 30th, you received reports in the BiH Presidency about the detention of Muslim civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you said that during June you were receiving other such reports from the media; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's why, at the June 30th meeting, you were aware and you talked about the crimes that were being committed by the Serb side; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In what I read out, there is no mention of any crimes. Inhumane conditions are discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You consider inhumane conditions not to be a crime? The maintenance of detention centres for civilians with inhumane conditions, you consider that not to be a crime?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, there is no room for me to take a personal stance on this. I'm only trying to say that if this report comes from the Serbian police about their own conduct, then it is credible. I can't know that better than they did. They knew what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so you don't dismiss Mr. Zupljanin's comments as propaganda, do you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, since they are discussing what they were doing, it would probably be ridiculous of me to say that they were launching propaganda against themselves. If Mr. Zupljanin is asserting this, he's actually addressing the activities of his organisation, of his institution. What other reaction should I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple answer to the question was: No, I do not dismiss these comments as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to close this topic, sir, you discuss in your statement your knowledge of detention facilities operated by Muslims in which Serbs were detained, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You do not discuss your knowledge of detention facilities operated by Serbs in which Muslims and Croats were detained, do you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat: I was in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo, Serbs did not keep Muslims in camps but the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you discuss knowledge of detention facilities operated by Serbs. Is that in your statement or is that not in your statement? That was the question. There may be good reasons for not having it in the statements because it didn't happen or whatever, but the question was whether you address detention facilities operated by Serbs in your statements. Mr. Mladic, one more word aloud and this is the last warning. Yes, yes, you know exactly what the consequences are. The last word you spoke allowed was "da" which means "yes," so you understood it. And this really is the last time. I don't want to have any interference with the testimony of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me put my question again, sir. You do not discuss your knowledge of detention facilities operated by Serbs in which Muslims and Croats were detained, in your statement, do you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only testify to what I have direct knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, last time: You're an intelligent man. You carefully listen to the question. Otherwise, one of the risks is that if you do not answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution and are always circumventing them, then your testimony, but then the whole of your testimony, might be given little or no weight. You should be aware of that. Apart from that, there is a duty to answer questions and not to comment on things that were not asked. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, it's very difficult for me to speak that way. I'm not used to it. I simply feel the need to explain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are not here to explain unless an explanation is asked by any question. The simple question was: Do you address in your statement your knowledge of Serb-operated detention facilities where others, other ethnicities, Muslims and/or Croats, were detained? Did you address that in your statement? Later on, in re-examination, Mr. Lukic will have ample opportunity to seek further explanation if he thinks he would need it. So therefore, don't start explaining what you consider to be relevant but just answer the questions. If you're not used to it, please get used to it now. Could you please answer that question, whether you address it in your statement. Simple "yes" or "no" would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be marked for identification pending CLSS reviewing the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 9723 receives number P6659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6659 is marked for identification pending verification of the translation. We take a break now, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Kecmanovic, you'll be escorted out of the courtroom. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think I set a deadline for the 16th of July for the tu quoque issue. Now, could it be that one of those witnesses will already be called on or before the 16th? In that case, for that witness, of course, we would like to receive your response or your reply earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Stojanovic just informed me that he should be here on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we would like to receive your response by Monday. That's the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should say the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning now to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you are going to turn to Sarajevo to the -- I have one question with in relation to what we discussed before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: After you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you said you received information by a person named Bosko Baskot. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had known him from before the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, when -- no, where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my request, he drafted a piece of text in which I intervened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Which I inserted in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't discuss it. Since I was asked by the Defence team in that case to say something about Prijedor, and having no direct knowledge about it, I turned to Mr. Bosko Baskot, asking him to write a short text in terms of how he saw it, and I simply integrated his piece of text into my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Into which report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where it appears for the first time. I don't recall any longer. I don't remember what case it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said earlier that you met him after you have testified in the Karadzic case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was a misunderstanding. I said that after the Karadzic case, I was in Banja Luka. While I was there, I heard from some people that things were not quite like Bosko wrote and in terms of what I had integrated in my text, in the sense that it was a bit blown out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that other people told you. You said: "I heard from some people." Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I can't identify them precisely. These were not targeted discussions or conversations, as was the case with Mr. Baskot, but en passant, when I met different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give me one name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You don't remember the names, but the information you gained from them was so important that you changed your testimony between the Karadzic testimony and this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I was present during such conversations. There was no targeted question in order to elicit a response or an explanation, but these were just conversations, some of which took place in cafes. I never went to see someone with the specific question in mind or no one came to see me but the topic simply surfaced in a conversation among people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions to follow up on His Honour's. First, if I suggested that that was your report for the Kvocka case, would that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, did you note in that report that one section had been drafted by someone else that had not been reviewed by you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I said any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But that's the testimony you've provided just now; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please let us be precise in terms of what I said. I said that I asked Bosko Baskot to write that part and of course I read it before integrating it into my next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me ask a more precise question, then. Did you note in that report that one section had been written by someone else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, we have it and we can check. You said you read it. Did you edit it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was so many years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think that completes my questions on this topic unless the Bench has anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to perhaps put a bit more pertinent question to you. Do I understand your testimony well that you submitted an expert report, part of which was written by a third person, without notifying anyone of that and without having properly verified the content, the accuracy, and the truth of what Mr. Baskot had written? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I'd like to answer with more than a mere "yes" or "no," to explain in a few sentences, because I recall that well. It was a general expert report. When I did that, the Defence team, however, asked me if possible to include the location of importance for that case, and I told them that I had no direct knowledge but that I could engage someone else similar to my capacity at the time as expert witness. I told them I could engage someone I knew who hailed from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm not interested in any way in the discussions you may have had with whatever Defence. I'm interested to know whether you presented a report, part of which was not authored by you but under your name and as part of your report, without being able to verify the accuracy of what that other person wrote and without mentioning that it was authored by someone else. I'm only interested in that. How it all happened is of no -- I'm not interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had confidence in that person and I integrated that text as my text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer simply is "yes" because -- I didn't ask for an explanation. You gave it voluntarily. Because you had confidence in a person. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow up on one of Judge Fluegge's questions. Sir, Judge Fluegge asked you what Mr. Baskot told you, you said he didn't tell you anything, you didn't discuss, he wrote a text for you. What did he write in the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That which is contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is it? Tell us what it is he wrote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had that a minute ago on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to the statement we had on our screen, or was that part of the report, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that was part of the witness's statement in the Karadzic case that addressed the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us now what exactly then it was that Mr. Baskot told you, Witness, or wrote, the content? Could you reproduce what he said? Or wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime ago you had on the screen indicated what was written there and there was the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have never seen this report. If it is exactly the same, if you say what was shown to you as part of your statement given in the Karadzic case, is that literally the same as we could find in your report? Is that exactly the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is so. I cannot claim with certainty but I think that was that. That was it, yes. I simply do not have that text which refers to that. I do believe that Mr. Prosecutor has the material pertaining to the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you wrote a report, you got information from different sources, one of which was Mr. Baskot. We don't want to read the whole report to find out what Baskot wrote. What is so difficult in you just telling us exactly what it is that Mr. Baskot said to you or wrote for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can tell, you have the text, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer my question, please. Don't talk to the Prosecutor. Just tell us exactly what Baskot told -- wrote for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly what we had on the screen one hour ago, ending with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What we had on the screen, we are told, is not the report that you're talking about. Mr. Traldi just told us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from memory I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- tell you. It was ten years ago, I believe. That those unsavorable incidents -- I think his note starts with explaining that two Serbian policemen were killed by, as far as I can remember, by a Muslim organised group. So there were two policemen, Serbian policemen, murdered. After that, there were -- there was repression against the Muslim population in Prijedor. This pertains to Prijedor. And then he further noted that there was different forms of repression ensuing. This is as far as I remember. Of course, repression against the Muslim population, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the Chamber would like to receive, either from Mr. Lukic or from you, the relevant parts of the report which was produced in the Kvocka case. Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can give you 65 ter numbers immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In our case, okay. If you would give that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1D2002 and 1D2003, and it's visible that those texts are different. So the other part, I guess, and maybe Professor could recognise it, is something that is added to the original expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be totally clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- my understanding is that 1D2002 is a portion of the expert report in the Kvocka case. We have uploaded the entirety as 30955. And 1D2003, unless I misread, is Mr. Kecmanovic's report in the Simic case. But I'm happy to have that double-checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can check it only with Mr. Kecmanovic. I cannot tell that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: They do have the case numbers on them which makes it a little bit easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are these long reports or are they -- and could the parties guide the Chamber in where to find in those reports the relevant sections for the matters on which he now changed his testimony compared with --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd suggest we try to do that at the break, Mr. President, if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Then one last question for the witness. Could you give us a bit more information about the person -- no, I don't need -- I don't need that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to -- one more question from me on this topic, sir. The information you included in the Kvocka report, though you didn't verify it, you did find it sufficiently reliable to provide to a court of law, right, in your capacity as an expert?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very small portion of the report, maybe 5 per cent, less than 10 per cent, if I remember correctly, and I -- that person who did that for me had my trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So for the record, you did, didn't you, find it sufficiently reliable to provide to a court of law in your capacity as an expert?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: The same as I used other sources, I saw that as being appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you about other sources. Are there other parts of your report which were written by other persons without stating that they were authored by others rather than by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then there were no other such portions because the report concerns the general situation about Sarajevo which I knew well. This particular portion concerned a locality that I was not familiar with. And this is why I went about it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In your report for the Simic case that addressed Bosanski Samac, there are sections that relate to events in that municipality. Did you draft those yourself or did you have someone more familiar with Bosanski Samac draft them for you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I spoke to people hailing from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so for the record, is your answer that you drafted those sections yourself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I consulted the people from the ground because I had not resided there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if you're done with this, I would have one additional question as well. Do you have a record of those interviews or conversations in the Simic report, with whom exactly you spoke, what they said to you, and what you used as a source for that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I, of course, had a sort of an archive, but whether I still have it at home in Belgrade, I don't know. I can't testify one way or the other. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you in the report state clearly what kind of sources you relied upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did not list the literature either. This is the way an expert report -- this is not a scientific paper where I would have to cite and quote and list literature, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there conversations in cafes, et cetera, as well, as source of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met with those people in different places, wherever it was convenient for them, and in certain cases it happened to be in cafes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you think that -- have you mentioned that, that part of your sources were just conversations with ordinary locals in pubs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, it was a long time ago. I can't remember those details, such -- I spoke with a number of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not my question but we can verify that in the report. Now, finally one question, you say: "... this is not a scientific paper where I would have to cite and quote and list literature, et cetera." Do you agree with me that citing and quoting literature is serving transparency and allows the reader to verify the accuracy of sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. But I was retained by the Defence team. I performed my mission in the way that they expected me to do it. And the Defence did not require of me to prepare my expert report in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you consider it of same importance for a court of law to have transparent information where the accuracy of the sources can be verified? Or do you consider that not important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know. I'm not a legal expert. I simply conferred with the Defence team and I complied with their requests in terms of the form of the report, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do want to turn now to Sarajevo, and as an initial question, you mentioned in your statement detention centres for Serbs. You've said you didn't mention detention centres where Muslims and Croats were held. Now, you heard about the detention centres where Serbs were held from other people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had immediate knowledge, direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, not for each and every one of them but for a large number of them, I had immediate knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have paragraphs 45 and 46 of the witness's statement on the screen? It's -- D556 is the exhibit number. And the whole section starting at 44 is valuable so if we can keep the whole page in the B/C/S on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I think, in paragraph 46 here, you suggest that you can talk personally about one private prison in the basement of the Zagreb Hotel but I put to you that in paragraph 45 --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not a hotel in Zagreb, the name of the hotel was Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Agreed. I put to you that in paragraph 45 you're speaking of private prisons more generally and you're saying: Based on the information we received from the people who came to us for help daily, we presented the specific complaints of Serbian citizens, which you also include in your statement. And then you note that the government formed a mixed commission to deal with the matter. Now, my question is: At least some of the information you've provided here is second-hand; correct? It relates to complaints of Serbian citizens.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people would come to the building of the Presidency and as victims they provided first-hand accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you received first-hand accounts. You are -- the information you're providing is not first-hand; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those with first-hand accounts would come to the building of the Presidency, and they were there to testify if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I think I understand your answer to be that you are not providing first-hand information yourself; right? You're talking about other people's experiences which you did not see, hear, smell or otherwise experience yourself.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that I was not the immediate victim and therefore that was not my experience or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I mean you're relating to us what other people told you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: To you here, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In -- both in the statement and in your testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be a logical trick, discussing what is first-hand and what is second-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like to stay away from logical tricks and I'd like to stick to the simple question I asked you. You're talking about other people's experiences which you didn't experience yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you've included what you heard about detention centres for Serbs but not what you heard about detention centres for Muslims or Croats in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a great deal of difference. I -- here in this case, I saw with my own eyes because I would visit those centres, Hotel Zagreb, Hotel Europa, I can list a number of localities, people who had been mistreated there would approach me to tell me about that. There were no Muslim victims of such treatment in terms of arrests, detention, investigation, mistreatment. That kind of victim, when it came to Muslims, did not exist in Sarajevo, at least in that part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the central government, where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to what you did experience in Sarajevo. And you experienced shelling, beginning in April and May of 1992, in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The citizens of Sarajevo were terrified by the shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were terrified yourself, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You and the other citizens feared for your lives, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, not feared for your lives but we were in danger and we were afraid. That's for sure. Simply, when shelling started, we would take shelter in houses, in basements. Not a single building was destroyed, but there were cases where missiles would penetrate a building through the window. But shelters in cellars, in basements, and edifices were shelter enough. Of course, people had to go about their daily errands, and during such periods there was this danger, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So if were you on the street during a shelling, you feared for your life; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in such a case people would enter the nearest building to avoid that immediate danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And yet people were killed and wounded in shelling while you were in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: People were killed and wounded in May 1992 in shellings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And continuing in June --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Continuing in June 1992? People were killed and wounded in shellings?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Serbian artillery laid waste to the central and old part of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: One couldn't say laid waste. I myself lived in that neighbourhood. There were many buildings that were hit, their facades were hit, but you couldn't say that the centre of the town was laid waste to. I lived all my life there. I had lived all my life there and I lived through that period there in Sarajevo. Those missiles were not such that they would destroy a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't want to quibble about specific language, but you yourself have written that the superior Serb artillery laid waste to the central and old part of Sarajevo, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just have to intervene because of the translation. It was differently translated so that's why now you have "yes" unlike before "laid waste" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. That is text that exists in both languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Unfortunately that report, the Office of the Prosecutor only has a copy of the English version, and so I don't have the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see that is what report, then, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We can call up the specific page if it would assist, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think if it's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30955. Now, for the B/C/S we only have the section dealing specifically with Prijedor municipality on the left. For the English we have a more complete report. Could we have page 29 in the English, please? And I don't have in my notes where it appears on the page. Can we perhaps turn to the next -- actually before we do, sorry, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the top of page 30. And we see a number, 29, in the bottom right-hand corner which apparently confused my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you read it again slowly and then Mr. Lukic will carefully listen. If there is any translation issue, we would like to deal with that once the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm interested in the second sentence: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste the central and old part of the city." Just that clause of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph, sorry, in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph under "Izetbegovic's martyred Olympic city," and it's the second sentence. I'll read it again so you can hear the translation. "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste the central and old part of the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are aware that you cannot compare it with the B/C/S version on the left-hand side. It's not the same text, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've put that on the record, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because here it's about Prijedor, on the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness should not read -- the witness should just carefully listen to what Mr. Traldi reads about the superior Serb artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only today during the translation "laid waste" was translated in two different ways --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- so that's maybe what created the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you are most happy with the translation -- the last interpretation? Then we would ask Mr. Traldi to read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very rarely I'm on B/C/S channel and I happened to be at that moment. Lately I was not listening to B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to have Mr. Lukic monitor it while I read it one more time if that would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste the central and old part of the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was the third translation of this and Mr. Traldi is using the same term all the time. I have to say that, but the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the next break, that one line will be -- in one way or another be verified as far as translation is concerned. And we kindly ask the assistance of CLSS to do so because this is exactly what we want to avoid, that is that during live interpretation, which is a different thing from sitting behind your desk with five dictionaries and checking every word in great detail, but perhaps for that one line, we could have that done in the next break. Perhaps we could take that break now, Mr. Traldi, so that you could immediately start if - which I'm still hopeful to expect - CLSS could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I hope so too. I wouldn't want to translate it myself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's very wise. Mr. Usher, could you -- we take a break, Witness, and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness will be brought in, the Chamber highly appreciates that CLSS was quite willing to help us, but of course there is one remaining problem. That is that we don't have the original. What we could do is to look at the English version, and that will be done I do understand within the next 15 minutes, that we then see whether there is one verified B/C/S translation for that. Later, you always can verify, Mr. Lukic, whether that corresponds with the B/C/S original which is not available, I do understand, to the Prosecution but most likely has to be found somewhere in the archives of the Kvocka case or -- unless you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was on Kvocka case but obviously Mr. Kecmanovic testified for somebody else because I left that case immediately after Kvocka finished his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But sooner or later I take that we'll be able to find a copy of that report, a full copy, in B/C/S. That's -- but let's proceed at this moment on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One exercise I would offer too, we can ask the witness which of the translations offered to him best describes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no way that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before he is here maybe you want to hear which translations he received. Always Mr. Traldi used "laid waste."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First translation was "razed to the ground;" second one is "damaged." To the first one he answered no. So although the question was "laid waste," the answer was "no." And then "laid waste" again, but now it was "damaged," and he said "yes." So that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, we leave it to that. And Mr. Traldi has an opportunity to put the question now, in 10, 15 minutes from now, guided by what CLSS -- but still not being sure that we have the -- whether it corresponds with the original. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Until we get the confirmed translation of that sentence, I'm going to ask a couple of other questions but about the same page of that report. So if we could have it back up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Serb artillery was superior to Muslim artillery; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, not to be disturbed, we should remove the B/C/S version on the screen because this page is not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That sounds like a very good suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Muslims could not threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements around the city, could they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: They could threaten them. One can clearly see it if we take Grbavica, for example. That part of Sarajevo was held by Serbs. Grbavica was destroyed although not to the extent the centre of town was. When I went there, I could see actually that the degree of destruction was very high or perhaps the degree of damage, to be quite precise. There was firing both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask a couple of questions to follow up on your answer. First, you say the degree of destruction was very high. Are you talking about Grbavica or about the centre of the city?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the centre of the city, you said, Grbavica wasn't destroyed to the extent the centre of town was, so Grbavica --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that. I said that both were destroyed. They are both part of the urban area. Pale is further away but Grbavica is still an integral part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like to stay away from geography. At lines 21 and 22, you were recorded to say -- lines 21 and 22, temporary page 69 --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't interrupt Mr. Traldi. Wait for his question and then answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At lines 21 and 22 of temporary transcript page 69, you were recorded to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm really sorry. I would ask for this audio to be checked. I think that the witness said the opposite what was recorded here. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. We are talking about page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 69, line 21 and 22, the end of line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you -- Mr. Traldi, perhaps you put the same question again to the witness. That is: "And the Muslims could not threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements around the city, could they?" That was the question. And we read as an answer: "They could threaten them. One can clearly see it if we take Grbavica, for example. That part of Sarajevo was held by Serbs. Grbavica was destroyed although not to the extent the centre of the town area." That is what was -- appears on our screen as what you are recorded -- what you -- what you said as recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is the President's recitation just now, is that a correct recitation of your evidence in response to my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not precise. May I repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The centre of Sarajevo is a rather large area. Grbavica is part of the urban area but it is only a neighbourhood of Sarajevo. The damage in that small neighbourhood were more visible than if you looked at the destruction spread out across the entire urban area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- the witness now apparently makes a comparison between Grbavica and the totality of the town. Not a comparison between Grbavica and the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm asking specifically for a comparison between Grbavica and Bascarsija, which is what I think you were -- which is what I think I'd been asking for before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to be very careful we are talking about old part of the town because you could refer to the old part of town, if I understand well - and I'm also looking at you, Mr. Lukic - as being the old city centre including Bascarsija or what is called Stari Grad which means, if I understand it well, the old town which is a municipality in the Sarajevo area. So whenever we use the word "old town," we should be very careful to be precise in what we refer to. And I do understand, Mr. Traldi, that you wanted the witness to compare the damage done to Grbavica on the one hand side and the old city centre including Bascarsija on the other side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you compare that, the damage done to those two parts of the town, Grbavica and the old city centre including Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was more destruction at Grbavica because it is a smaller area, and the fire was focused on that small area. As regards Stari Grad, including Bascarsija where I lived, there was less destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stari Grad understood as limited to the old city centre, therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the municipality. The old city centre including Bascarsija, the old part of the town, not the entire opstina or municipality of Stari Grad but just the city centre, the densely populated city centre. Could you please compare these two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could see the damage more, it was more visible in Grbavica than one could see in the old nucleus of the city, as you put it precisely. Not all of the Stari Grad municipality but the inner city, including Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question: Was this the case notwithstanding the superior Serbian artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This statement that is being quoted to you, this sentence, starts by saying: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste" -- okay, I'm not talking about waste. Now, when you say "superior Serbian artillery," superior to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As compared with the artillery nests existing in the very centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question then is: Notwithstanding the fact that the Serbian artillery was superior, are you saying that it caused less damage than inferior artillery? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said "no" as an answer to the question that -- Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in answer to my question a couple of moments ago you said, yes, the Muslims could threaten Serbian artillery emplacements around the city and then you mentioned Grbavica. Did you mean Grbavica, a neighbourhood, or Grbavica as -- or to suggest that Grbavica was a location of Serbian artillery emplacements?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was or not. I don't know if there was a Serbian artillery in Grbavica but I do know that Grbavica was targeted from Sarajevo city, from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me ask the question that I'd meant to ask then very specifically. The Muslim army was not able to threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements positioned on hills around the edge of the city, were they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, although I am no military expert, I think they did threaten those emplacements and they could do so. The distance was the same, even if one looked from the Serbian positions or the other way around. If they could reach one another from one direction, they could have reached one another from the other. The distance was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at your expert report that's still on the screen in front of us and setting aside the geometry of artillery firing, the last sentence of the first paragraph starts: "Of course, not even when weapons started arriving in larger quantities from Islamic countries," then it explains some ways that they arrived, and then it ends, "was it enough for the Muslim army to threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements positioned on hills around the edge of the city." So what you've said in that report is that even after receiving additional arms, the Serbian artillery -- the Muslim army, rather, was not able to threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have a look at the sentence itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can read English, don't you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not there in B/C/S at this moment. So you're able to read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll slowly read the whole of the sentence. It reads as follows: "Of course, not even when weapons started arriving in larger quantities from Islamic countries, in humanitarian aid containers which landed unobstructed at UN-controlled Sarajevo airport or when they dug a 'secret' passage under the airport tarmac, was it enough for the Muslim army to threaten the Serbian artillery emplacements positioned on hills around the edge of the city." So even when those larger quantities arrived, they were not able, it was not enough for the Muslim army to have threatened the Serbian artillery emplacements positioned on the hills.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question now. This issue of threatening had to do with breaking through the ring. The Muslim forces in Sarajevo tried incessantly to break through the artillery encirclement around Sarajevo. In that sense, I said it wasn't enough. They kept trying and never succeeded throughout the war. There were constant attacks from Sarajevo, from the city towards the outer ring, and even the weapons that arrived did not assist in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we've received from CLSS a translation of the sentence in question and I'd ask the usher's assistance to distribute a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For as good as it is. Perhaps -- we may not conclude the testimony of the witness today. Perhaps you could give it a try to find the original B/C/S version. Not to say that I stop you here at this moment but that at least when the witness is still there that we have it verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have a copy of your Kvocka expert report with you, do you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but archives in this Tribunal might. Was it presented as an exhibit in the Kvocka case, Mr. -- at least it's worthwhile finding out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not in this case but in the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kvocka case. I understood that Professor was expert witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so therefore it must be somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I left before anybody else except my client started his defence so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, I'm not addressing you, but if an expert report is admitted into evidence, then it usually is somewhere available, either in electronic form or in hard copy form, and then we could get hold of it and avoid further discussions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree that we are in an unusual situation, Mr. President. I think what I meant to be suggesting was we've done fairly extensive searches of the electronic databases without finding it and the same occurred before the witness testified in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was not found?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right. It's not on JDB in the B/C/S, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In hard copy? If it has an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I haven't been into the archives so we can check that overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we continue now, as in the way you suggested, and you make an effort to find it in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic confirm he's had a chance to review the translation that was passed over?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this is the most harsh translation possible for -- possible for this term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For your case you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not for my case. I wouldn't say it's the proper translation either. But you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But this now has been verified, the one line, and if you want to have it verified again, tomorrow we will hear more. We will proceed on this basis which is the best we have at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Actually I think it might be valuable for a copy to be provided to the booth, if it hasn't been. So that it can be read to the witness in this format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the booth is not yet informed about this. Meanwhile you can perhaps continue with another topic, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Speaking of the balance of forces around Sarajevo, you've mentioned the Serb artillery was superior. It's right that the VRS also had an advantage in weapons taken over from the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: It had officers who were better educated, and it had a better commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the question was not -- it was about weapons. A commander is not a weapon. Trained staff is not a weapon. Please answer the question. And don't put forward what seems to be your case rather than -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the question is actually not properly posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, has an advantage that then [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness should first be asked whether he knows what was left to the VRS, what was left to Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that may --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He's asked to compare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness talks about persons. The question was, right or wrong, was clearly about weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You should have done that to start with instead of intervening when I admonished the witness that he should focus on the question that is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you please introduce the matter by asking the witness what he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I might, I'd call up page 33 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could zoom in towards the bottom of the page. So I'm reading again from the witness's expert report and the paragraph right above the words "the NATO intervention and the Dayton Agreement." The last sentence reads: "Their advantage in weapons taken over from the JNA and in an officer corps trained in one of the best armies in the region gave General Ratko Mladic a substantial edge in the battlefield, while the Croats and particularly the Muslims earned the status of the weaker side which the big, strong world had the moral obligation to help survive."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So that's the foundation for my question. And I put to you again, sir, the VRS had an advantage in weapons taken over from the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: If it's not a problem, I would like to ask you to put forward a statement in the form of a question and not as a statement, affirmative statement. If it's not problem, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll put again to you, the VRS had an advantage in weapons taken over from the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is how I -- what I wrote, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is a portion of the report that you drafted, right? I see you've nodded but you have to articulate your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the booth has the translation that's been provided by CLSS so if we could go back now to page 30 at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for your information, the Chamber is informed about the three ways in which -- the three different versions that -- just for you to know that we are aware of it. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'm going to be reading again the second sentence of the top paragraph: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste the central and old part of the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it? That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: That happened, but there is this word "damage," "destroy," "laid waste," therefore it's relative or could be relative. But the gist of that sentence stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Serbian forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the Krajisnik case there was a misunderstanding concerning that particular point. In Sarajevo, we could not tell incoming and outgoing detonations apart, and whatever explosion we heard, we thought that it was coming from the Serbian side. Only later did we find out that this was not so. Another thing I would like to point out is that this was not drafted as a report for the Court. It's an authored paper, text, which may be imprecise in parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about what you said in the Krajisnik case about the question I just asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30941?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's your Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm looking for page 173 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tieger's question begins at the very last line of this page and he says: "Isn't it correct, and haven't you said previously, that Serbian" - we will turn the page - "forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills? Back to that question?" And you answered: "Yes. That was my impression." That was your testimony, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I emphasise this was my impression of a person who at that time resided and lived in Sarajevo, and this is why I have to emphasise this difference between an impression and fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was your experience; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it was -- it was living with --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was living with that sense that your city was being randomly showered with shells that terrified you, as you said earlier, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what it also reads, yes. Of course. How could it be any different?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn last today to one other topic related to Sarajevo. Maybe it will be brief enough that I'll get to do one more thing after, but you assert in paragraph 52 of your statement that General MacKenzie made allegations about Muslims shooting at their own people in Sarajevo. And you state in paragraph 52: "I have not read MacKenzie's book and I do not know what evidence he presented." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not need MacKenzie's book. I was in Sarajevo when he issued that statement at a press conference in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'll take from your answer that you have not read his book; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I ask because in your testimony in the Krajisnik case, eight years ago, it was put to you that General MacKenzie had denied, both in his book and in his interviews, making exactly the suggestions that you've repeated in your statement. And you said you hadn't read his book and didn't know what it said. Now, you still don't know what General MacKenzie has said about this in his book, do you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know reliably what he said when he was in Sarajevo at the time, and that statement of his caused and engendered a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of Muslim politicians in the audience. What he stated later in his life, that I don't know, or what he stated in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was that you still do not know what General MacKenzie has said about this in his book. So what he states in his book. Why not answer that question to start with? No, you don't know what he said about it in his book. Is that your answer? Because you were not asked about what he said in Sarajevo. You were asked about what he said about this in his book. Do you know it or do you still do not know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would have been the short answer to the question which was very clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 159 of this same document. I'm looking for line 16 and below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was put to you was: "That's absolutely false and you know it, sir. General MacKenzie has been at great pains, both in his book and his interviews, to make clear that he was not in a position to assert that Bosnian Muslim forces were responsible for such atrocities. You know that." And in the answer, you said you hadn't read his book and you didn't know what it says there, but you remembered an interview he had given in Sarajevo during the war. So you were told then that were you mischaracterising his position based on his book and his interviews after the war and you haven't checked to see whether that's true in the intervening eight years, have you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one intervention here. I do not accept this way of discussing these matters. I came here on a voluntary basis to help the Court and whenever I left the Court, I received thanks about helping the Court. This time round, the Prosecutor claims that I know that I said I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you do not feel comfortable and happy with what happens at this moment. If there are reasons to intervene, the Defence will do so. The Defence has called you as a witness. It is the Chamber who controls and who supervises the examination of witnesses. If we consider that something inappropriate happens, we will intervene. If we overlook something, Mr. Lukic will intervene. The best way of assisting the Court, and that is you said you wanted to do, is to answer the questions, having carefully listened to them and directly. That is what you're expected to do. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think you recall the question, sir. I'll put to you again that you haven't checked to see whether your description of General MacKenzie's position is correct in the eight years since your Krajisnik testimony, have you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute ago, you claimed that I knew that and that I claimed that I didn't know it, and this is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer the question. Have you verified it in those eight years or have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not verified. I had no need to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the answer to the question. It's even more, whether there was any need is a different matter. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to turn to a different topic. I note that it's about time to end for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn for the day. Witness, before you leave the courtroom I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given, and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning. And I give you the following thought to consider. That is that you just should answer the questions and not what is relevant and what needs to be explained is for the parties primarily, and to some extent also for the Chamber, to determine. As a witness, you have to follow this determination of what we consider relevant and let's not forget, it's Prosecution, it's also Defence, and it's also the Chamber. Please keep that in mind because this Chamber has observed that you are in 60, 70 per cent of the cases, you're either not directly answering the question or that you're adding a lot of things that were not asked. If it's relevant, further questions will follow, either by the Prosecution or by the Defence. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You may follow the usher.
